hints: Look at what is happening to sulfur in the second reaction, it starts as +6 in sulfuric acid but ends up as +4, 0 and -2.
Notice that both reactions start the same way by making HX, but only HI goes on to react further to give $\text{I}_2$.
Think about which halide ion can give away electrons more easily to reduce the sulfuric acid while itself being oxidised.
walkthrough:
**Spot the first common reaction**

Both solids first do a simple acid-base reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid to make the hydrogen halide.

$$\text{NaX} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HX}$$

**Compare what happens next**

With NaCl it stops there, we just see $\text{HCl}$. With NaI the $\text{HI}$ that forms does not survive, we see $\text{I}_2$ plus reduced sulfur products like $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.

$$2\text{HI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Explain with reducing strength**

This extra step is redox. Sulfuric acid is an oxidising agent and $\text{I}^-$ is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce it, being oxidised itself from -1 in $\text{I}^-$ to 0 in $\text{I}_2$.

$\text{Cl}^-$ is a much weaker reducing agent, so it cannot reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and no further reaction occurs. That difference in reducing power explains all the extra products.

options.A: Incorrect. Chloride is actually less reactive as a reducing agent and cannot displace iodine in this context. In halogen displacement, the more reactive halogen displaces the less reactive one, so chlorine displaces iodine, not chloride displacing iodine.
options.B: Incorrect. Volatility is not the cause of the extra products. Both $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HI}$ are volatile gases, but only $\text{HI}$ is oxidised further by the acid to give $\text{I}_2$, $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
options.C: Correct. Iodide ions are larger and lose electrons more easily than chloride ions, so they are stronger reducing agents. They reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (S from +6 to +4, 0 and -2) while being oxidised to $\text{I}_2$.
options.D: Incorrect. Dehydration means removing water from a substance, as with carbohydrates or hydrated salts. Here sulfuric acid is acting as an oxidising agent, gaining electrons and being reduced, not as a dehydrating agent.
